newsitem.title: FINLAND: KOROMA SAYS NO GUARANTEES OF STATUS QUO IN EMU.
newsitem.headline: KOROMA SAYS NO GUARANTEES OF STATUS QUO IN EMU.

text.p: There are no guarantees that all benefits gained by Finnish trade unioins will remain untouched in EMU, Johannes Koroma, director-general of the Confederation of Finnish Industry and Employers (TT) said on Friday.
"In the case of EMU there is no insurance policy which would guarantee that all the benefits gained would remain unchanged in the future," Koroma said in a prepared speech.
"No government or employer can give such a guarantee," he added.
"And the trade unions can not expect to get any such guarantee and no such guarantee has been negotiated."
The benefits brought by membership of European economic and monetary union (EMU) will have to be earned and the risks have to be avoided accordingly, Koroma said.

But he said that a planned joint resolution by the labour market organisations on the effects of monetary union could be justified in order to stress the importance of low inflation and to ease unfounded fears.
The organisations have negotiated about such a joint resolution but its contents are still open.

There are no plans to change current labour market rules or lower wages -- which have been agreed in pay deals -- as long as all the parties are ready to change their conduct and adapt to life in EMU, Koroma said.

"It means a commitment to low inflation and moderate wage rises, increased productivity and competitiveness and the strenghtening of corporate balance sheets, expansion of local pay deals and increasing purchasing power also by easing taxation," he said.

The labour market organisations agreed that the EMU decision should be kept apart from next year's pay deal talks, Koroma said, adding that EMU was a national, political decision and not a labour market question.
He said there had been no discussions yet on the timetable or content of collective bargaining talks on next year's pay deal.
"SAK's (Central Organisation of Finnish Trade Unions) internal situation is unclear to the point that no estimates of the (pay talks') content can be made for several months," Koroma said.
Competition will become tougher regardeless of Finnish EMU membership, Koroma said, adding that the core idea of EMU was to change economic conduct -- to live within one's means.
Adjusting to moderate inflation will not be easy for the trade unions accustomed to hefty wage rises, or for businesses used to having their debts eaten up by inflation, he said.
"When joining EMU, the reality is that wage levels in Finland and particularly net wages are not above other EU-countries," he said, adding:
"And another reality is that problems regarding EMU will not be solved by any buffer funds."
